title: Exact multi-objective LTL achievability in stochastic games
formal: Is exact multi-objective probabilistic LTL achievability decidable for finite full-observation turn-based stochastic games? Given such a rational game \(G\) with initial state \(s_0\), a finite list of LTL formulas \(\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_m\), and rational thresholds \(p_i\in[0,1]\), decide whether \[\exists\sigma\ \forall\tau\ \forall i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:\quad \Pr_{G,s_0}^{\sigma,\tau}(\varphi_i)\ge p_i.\] Both players may use arbitrary randomized strategies with unbounded history dependence. One deterministic algorithm must halt with the exact answer on every input. This is the decision target selected by the user on 16 September 2026 from the source's broader synthesis question.
why: A controller often has several probabilistic requirements, such as reliability and eventual response, that must hold under the same policy against an adversarial environment. Exact achievability asks whether the stated requirements can all be guaranteed, including boundary thresholds that approximation alone may not decide. It is a central decision component of quantitative synthesis for stochastic systems.

sentences: A finite stochastic game combines controller choices, adversary choices and rational chance transitions.
The selected question asks whether one randomized strategy can meet all supplied rational probability bounds for LTL properties against every adversary.
Both players may depend on the whole history, and the existential strategy need not have an effective finite representation.
The decision must distinguish actual exact threshold attainment from approximate or limit-sure guarantees.
This user-selected decision subproblem makes one part of the broader multi-objective synthesis programme precise.

definitions:
The finite state set \(S\) is partitioned into controller states \(S_1\), adversary states \(S_2\), and chance states \(S_c\), with a designated \(s_0\in S\). At a player state \(s\), a nonempty finite set \(E(s)\subseteq S\) lists the legal next states. At a chance state \(s\), the table \(P(s,t)\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\) sums to one over \(t\in S\). A play starts at \(s_0\) and continues forever: its owner chooses a legal successor at a player state, and a successor is sampled from \(P(s,\cdot)\) at a chance state. Terminal behavior is represented by a self-loop. There is no stopping, acyclicity, finite-horizon, partial-observation or bounded-memory promise. A finite set \(AP\) of atomic propositions and a labelling \(\ell:S\to2^{AP}\) are supplied. All state partitions, edges, labels and rational probabilities are explicit finite tables; indices and rational numerators/positive denominators are binary encoded.

A controller strategy assigns to each finite legal state history ending in \(S_1\) a probability distribution on that last state's legal successors; adversary strategies are defined symmetrically for \(S_2\). Both players observe the complete state history. Distribution values may be arbitrary real numbers, and dependence on the entire finite history is unrestricted. Strategies are abstract mathematical functions: the quantifiers impose no rationality, computability or finite-memory requirement on them. The same controller strategy must meet all objectives against every adversary. The decision algorithm receives only the finite game, formulas and thresholds; a strategy is not an input or a required output. For a fixed pair of strategies, cylinder probabilities are the products of the corresponding transition probabilities along finite histories, defining the usual probability measure on infinite plays.

An LTL formula has finite syntax \(\varphi::=\top\mid a\mid\neg\varphi\mid(\varphi\land\varphi)\mid X\varphi\mid(\varphi U\varphi)\), for \(a\in AP\). It is interpreted on the infinite label sequence of the play, from position zero. An atom holds at position \(j\) if it belongs to \(\ell(s_j)\); Boolean connectives have their ordinary meaning; \(X\varphi\) holds at \(j\) if \(\varphi\) holds at \(j+1\); and \(\varphi U\psi\) holds at \(j\) if some finite \(k\ge j\) satisfies \(\psi\) and every position from \(j\) through \(k-1\) satisfies \(\varphi\). Thus until is strong, not weak. These events are measurable. Formula trees and the finite objective list are explicit input; their sizes are unbounded. The empty list, if supplied, is vacuously achievable.

Each displayed threshold is non-strict. An upper bound \(\Pr(\varphi)\le p\) can be represented as the lower bound \(\Pr(\neg\varphi)\ge1-p\), so these upper bounds require no separate semantic convention. Achievability means an actual strategy attaining all bounds, not membership in the closure of achievable vectors or existence of a different strategy for every positive tolerance. The sought machine is uniform, has no oracle or advice, uses ordinary exact finite computation and may take any finite running time. Its YES/NO output has no random error or numerical tolerance. A malformed encoding may be rejected.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean proof of a total computable exact decision procedure for the displayed predicate, or prove that no such procedure exists. The positive proof must formalize finite rational games, full-history real-valued strategy quantifiers, the induced play measure, LTL semantics, termination and both answer directions. A negative proof must preserve this complete-observation turn-based finite rational class and allow the stated randomized strategies. Deciding only pure or finite-memory strategies, qualitative thresholds, stopping games, approximate Pareto membership or limit-sure achievability does not settle the target. A decision answer is sufficient for the selected scope; computing an effective strategy witness is a separate synthesis requirement not selected here. This review supplies no Lean proof of a resolution.

context_blocks.text: The original source asks for strategy synthesis, which includes producing a strategy. On 16 September 2026 the user selected the narrower exact decision task: determine whether any permitted controller strategy exists, with no effective representation of a witness required. This scope change is explicit; it is not attributed to the historical sentence as an equivalent formulation.

Different requirements can conflict because the controller must use one policy. Solving each scalar objective using its own optimal strategy does not establish simultaneous achievability. The quantifier order puts that shared policy before the universally quantified adversary.

The 2016 overview separates verification, strategy synthesis and approximation. It records that memory requirements can be unbounded in multi-objective problems and gives approximation results under stopping assumptions. Neither a restricted strategy representation nor a stopping condition has been imported into the selected general model.

Approximation can identify vectors close to the achievable region while leaving exact boundary membership unresolved. The selected non-strict inequalities require actual attainment; replacing every threshold by a slightly easier one and using different strategies would answer a different question.

Graf–Lin–Majumdar establish PSPACE-completeness for conjunctions of almost-sure and nonzero reachability/safety requirements and other qualitative fragments. This is substantial progress for restricted objectives. It does not by itself decide arbitrary rational probability bounds on general LTL formulas.

The 2026 paper also distinguishes Boolean combinations, determinacy and randomized versus pure strategies. Its undecidability discussion for deterministic strategies cannot be transferred to the larger randomized existential strategy class. No checked primary result found in the September search resolves the exact selected predicate.
